# Aim of this notebook

This notebook prepares the NHANES 2021–2023 dataset for the analyses in parts 2–4. The theme of our project is **obesity in US adults**: who is at risk (part 2), which laboratory profile accompanies it (part 3), and whether it can be predicted from that profile (part 4). Following the guiding questions of the assignment, we:

1. describe the structure of the data (samples, features, variable types);
2. define the study population;
3. find and handle quality problems (special codes, top-coding, missing values, outliers);
4. select and transform the laboratory features with justified, label-independent criteria;
5. check with a PCA whether samples cluster by biology or by technical factors;
6. save the preprocessed data for the next parts.

Every preprocessing decision is motivated in the text directly above or below the code that implements it.

# Packages and data

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)       # data wrangling and ggplot2
library(ggpubr)          # QQ plots and arranging plots
library(ComplexHeatmap)  # correlation heatmap

theme_set(theme_classic())
```

Change `data_dir` to the folder that contains the two csv files on your own computer. All other paths are built from it.

```{r paths}
data_dir <- "C:/Users/achil/OneDrive/Documenten/AJ 2026-2027/Semester 1/Large Scale Analysis of Biomedical Data/Group Project"
```

Two files were provided:

- `NHANES_20212023_merged_filtered 1.csv`: the data. One row per participant (`SEQN`), one column per variable. Several NHANES 2021–2023 files (demographics, examination, laboratory, questionnaire) were merged on `SEQN`.
- `NHANES_20212023_codebook_filtered 1.csv`: one row per column of the data, with a readable label, the original NHANES file and the component.

`guess_max` is set high because many columns are empty in the first rows (e.g. subsample measurements). With the default (1000 rows), `read_csv()` could guess such a column as "logical" and silently turn the later values into `NA`. The codebook contains a few non-UTF-8 characters (e.g. µ), so it is read as latin1.

```{r load}
nhanes_raw <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "NHANES_20212023_merged_filtered 1.csv"),
                       guess_max = 12000, show_col_types = FALSE)
codebook <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "NHANES_20212023_codebook_filtered 1.csv"),
                     locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"), show_col_types = FALSE)

dim(nhanes_raw)
dim(codebook)

# Does the codebook describe exactly the columns of the data, in the same order?
all(colnames(nhanes_raw) == codebook$variable)

# Is every participant present only once?
anyDuplicated(nhanes_raw$SEQN) == 0
```

# Structure of the data

## Samples and features

The raw data contain 11,933 participants and 486 variables. The codebook groups the variables into four NHANES components:

```{r components}
codebook %>% count(component, sort = TRUE)

codebook %>%
  count(component, file, name = "n_variables") %>%
  arrange(component, desc(n_variables))
```

Almost all columns are stored as numbers, also the categorical ones: NHANES codes categories as integers (e.g. `RIAGENDR`: 1 = male, 2 = female). The only text column is `BPAOARM` (arm used for the blood pressure measurement, "R"/"L").

```{r column-classes}
table(sapply(nhanes_raw, class))
```

## Variable types

The codebook does not tell us the variable type. As a first overview of **all** 486 variables, we classify them by their role and by the number of distinct values:

- identifier, survey design variables and comment codes are recognised from their name or label;
- variables with only 2 distinct values are binary;
- variables with 3–15 distinct values are integer codes for categories;
- variables with more than 15 distinct values are numeric measurements.

```{r type-overview}
n_values <- sapply(nhanes_raw, function(x) length(unique(na.omit(x))))

type_tbl <- codebook %>%
  mutate(n_values = n_values[variable],
         type = case_when(
           variable == "SEQN" ~ "identifier",
           str_starts(variable, "WT") | str_starts(variable, "SDMV") ~ "survey design (weight, stratum, PSU)",
           str_detect(label, regex("comment|cmt|comt", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "comment code (quality flag)",
           n_values <= 1 ~ "constant or empty",
           n_values == 2 ~ "binary (nominal)",
           n_values <= 15 ~ "categorical codes (nominal or ordinal)",
           TRUE ~ "numeric (continuous or discrete)"))

table(type_tbl$type, type_tbl$component)

# Variables without any information
type_tbl %>% filter(type == "constant or empty") %>% select(variable, label, n_values)
```

The majority (237) are numeric measurements, mostly in the laboratory component, and 84 are binary or categorical codes. 155 variables are not features: the identifier, 31 survey design variables and 123 comment codes. Ten variables are constant or empty and carry no information. Examples are the data release cycle (the same for everyone), three volatile organic compounds that are always below the detection limit, and questions about the first milk fed to infants.

The number of distinct values cannot tell whether categories are ordered or whether a number is a count. For the variables we use, we therefore determined the type from the NHANES documentation pages of each file (e.g. `DEMO_L.htm`): The meaning of the codes was taken from the NHANES documentation pages of each file (e.g. `DEMO_L.htm`).

```{r variable-types, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~variable,  ~description,                                ~type,
  "SEQN",     "Participant identifier",                    "identifier (not a feature)",
  "RIAGENDR", "Sex (1 = male, 2 = female)",                "nominal (binary)",
  "RIDRETH3", "Race/Hispanic origin incl. NH Asian",       "nominal (6 categories)",
  "DMDEDUC2", "Education level, adults 20+",               "ordinal (5 levels)",
  "RIDEXMON", "Six-month exam period (Nov–Apr / May–Oct)", "nominal (binary)",
  "PHDSESNZ", "Exam session (morning / afternoon-evening)","nominal (binary)",
  "RIDAGEYR", "Age in years (top-coded at 80)",            "discrete (continuous in practice)",
  "INDFMPIR", "Family income-to-poverty ratio (top-coded at 5)", "continuous",
  "ALQ121",   "Alcohol frequency past 12 months (0–10 categories)", "ordinal",
  "ALQ130",   "Average number of drinks per drinking day", "discrete (count)",
  "BMXBMI",   "Body mass index (kg/m²)",                   "continuous",
  "BPXOSY1-3","Systolic blood pressure, 3 readings",       "continuous",
  "LBX...",   "Laboratory measurements",                   "continuous (mostly right-skewed)",
  "LBD...LC", "Laboratory comment codes (0 = at/above, 1 = below detection limit)", "nominal (binary), quality flag",
  "WT...",    "Survey sample weights",                     "design variable (not a feature)"
) %>% knitr::kable()
```

# Study population

We restrict the analyses to:

1. **participants who were interviewed and examined** (`RIDSTATR` = 2). The 3,073 participants who were only interviewed have no body measurements, blood pressure or laboratory data.
2. **adults aged 20 years or older**. Children have different reference values for BMI and blood pressure and are not asked most adult questions. Education (`DMDEDUC2`) is only available from age 20, and Flegal et al. (2010) use the same cut-off.
3. **non-pregnant participants** (`RIDEXPRG` ≠ 1). Pregnancy strongly changes body weight, blood volume and many laboratory values (e.g. hormones, hemoglobin). Flegal et al. also excluded pregnant women.

`!(RIDEXPRG %in% 1)` keeps participants with a missing pregnancy status (all men and women outside the 20–44 age range in which the question is asked).

```{r population}
flow <- tibble(
  step = c("All participants",
           "Interviewed and examined (RIDSTATR = 2)",
           "... and aged 20 years or older",
           "... and not pregnant"),
  n = c(nrow(nhanes_raw),
        sum(nhanes_raw$RIDSTATR == 2),
        sum(nhanes_raw$RIDSTATR == 2 & nhanes_raw$RIDAGEYR >= 20),
        sum(nhanes_raw$RIDSTATR == 2 & nhanes_raw$RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
              !(nhanes_raw$RIDEXPRG %in% 1)))
)
knitr::kable(flow)

nhanes <- nhanes_raw %>%
  filter(RIDSTATR == 2, RIDAGEYR >= 20, !(RIDEXPRG %in% 1))
```

The study population contains **6,023 adults**.

# Special codes and top-coding

## Special codes

In the questionnaire and demographic variables, NHANES uses codes such as 7/77/777 ("refused") and 9/99/999 ("don't know"). They look like numbers but are not measurements: an average number of 999 drinks per day is meaningless. The code depends on the number of digits of the variable, so we first inspect the values and then define the codes per variable.

```{r special-codes-inspect}
# Example: the codes only appear as a separate group of values far above the real range
table(nhanes$DMDEDUC2, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes$ALQ130, useNA = "ifany")
```

```{r special-codes}
special_codes <- list(
  DMDEDUC2 = c(7, 9),     DMDMARTZ = c(77, 99),   DMDBORN4 = c(77, 99),
  DMQMILIZ = c(7, 9),     DMDYRUSR = c(77, 99),   ALQ111   = c(7, 9),
  ALQ121   = c(77, 99),   ALQ130   = c(777, 999), ALQ142   = c(77, 99),
  ALQ270   = c(77, 99),   ALQ280   = c(77, 99),   ALQ151   = c(7, 9),
  ALQ170   = c(777, 999)
)

# Count how many values will be recoded, before recoding them
recode_summary <- tibble(
  variable  = names(special_codes),
  codes     = map_chr(special_codes, ~ paste(.x, collapse = "/")),
  n_recoded = map_int(names(special_codes), ~ sum(nhanes[[.x]] %in% special_codes[[.x]]))
)
knitr::kable(recode_summary)

# Replace the special codes by NA
for (v in names(special_codes)) {
  nhanes[[v]][nhanes[[v]] %in% special_codes[[v]]] <- NA
}
```

Only a few values per variable are affected (at most 33, for the time living in the US). Because they are so rare, we simply treat them as missing.

## Top-coding

Two variables are top-coded for privacy reasons. These are not errors, but they limit the interpretation:

- `RIDAGEYR` = 80 means "80 years or older" (`r sum(nhanes$RIDAGEYR == 80)` participants);
- `INDFMPIR` = 5 means "income at least 5 times the poverty level" (`r sum(nhanes$INDFMPIR == 5, na.rm = TRUE)` participants).

We keep these values. In regression models, the effect of age above 80 and of high incomes will therefore be underestimated slightly.

# Derived and recoded variables

We convert the coded categorical variables to factors with readable labels, and derive the variables needed in parts 2–4:

- **Race/ethnicity**: non-Hispanic White, the largest group, is the reference level, as in Flegal et al.
- **Education** is an ordered factor.
- **Blood pressure**: the mean of the (up to) three oscillometric readings, as in Micha et al. and notebook 3. `rowMeans()` returns `NaN` when all three readings are missing; we turn that into `NA`.
- **BMI categories** use the WHO cut-offs: overweight 25–29.9, obesity ≥ 30. Obesity (BMI ≥ 30) is the outcome of part 2 and the contrast of part 3.
- **Abdominal obesity**: waist circumference > 102 cm in men or > 88 cm in women. BMI does not show where fat is stored, so this alternative definition will be used as a sensitivity analysis.
- **Smoking status** is derived from serum cotinine, a breakdown product of nicotine: cotinine ≥ 3 ng/mL = current smoker. This objective measure does not depend on self-report. Cotinine was not kept as a laboratory feature (section 8: a large share of the values is below the detection limit, which is exactly what makes it a good marker of non-smoking). Smoking is a confounder in part 3, because it affects inflammation markers and white blood cells.

```{r derive}
nhanes <- nhanes %>%
  mutate(
    sex       = factor(RIAGENDR, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    race_eth  = factor(RIDRETH3, levels = c(3, 1, 2, 4, 6, 7),
                       labels = c("NH White", "Mexican American", "Other Hispanic",
                                  "NH Black", "NH Asian", "Other/multiracial")),
    education = factor(DMDEDUC2, levels = 1:5, ordered = TRUE,
                       labels = c("<9th grade", "9-11th grade", "High school/GED",
                                  "Some college/AA", "College graduate+")),
    age_group = cut(RIDAGEYR, breaks = c(20, 40, 60, Inf), right = FALSE,
                    labels = c("20-39", "40-59", "60+")),
    exam_period  = factor(RIDEXMON, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Nov-Apr", "May-Oct")),
    # PHDSESNZ: 0 = morning, 1 = afternoon/evening (FASTQX_L documentation)
    exam_session = factor(PHDSESNZ, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Morning", "Afternoon/evening")),
    sbp = rowMeans(pick(BPXOSY1, BPXOSY2, BPXOSY3), na.rm = TRUE),
    dbp = rowMeans(pick(BPXODI1, BPXODI2, BPXODI3), na.rm = TRUE),
    sbp = if_else(is.nan(sbp), NA_real_, sbp),
    dbp = if_else(is.nan(dbp), NA_real_, dbp),
    bmi_cat = cut(BMXBMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, Inf), right = FALSE,
                  labels = c("Underweight", "Normal weight", "Overweight", "Obese")),
    obese = factor(if_else(BMXBMI >= 30, "Obese", "Not obese"),
                   levels = c("Not obese", "Obese")),
    abdominal_obese = factor(
      if_else((sex == "Male" & BMXWAIST > 102) | (sex == "Female" & BMXWAIST > 88),
              "Abdominal obesity", "No abdominal obesity"),
      levels = c("No abdominal obesity", "Abdominal obesity")),
    smoker = factor(if_else(LBXCOT >= 3, "Smoker", "Non-smoker"),
                    levels = c("Non-smoker", "Smoker"))
  )

# Sample sizes per group
nhanes %>% count(sex)
nhanes %>% count(race_eth)
nhanes %>% count(age_group)
nhanes %>% count(bmi_cat)
nhanes %>% count(smoker)

# Agreement between the two obesity definitions
table(BMI = nhanes$obese, waist = nhanes$abdominal_obese)
```

# Missing values

## Where are the missing values?

We calculate the percentage of missing values of every variable in the study population and summarise it per NHANES file.

```{r missing}
missing_tbl <- tibble(variable    = colnames(nhanes_raw),
                      pct_missing = colMeans(is.na(nhanes[, colnames(nhanes_raw)])) * 100) %>%
  left_join(codebook, by = "variable")

missing_by_file <- missing_tbl %>%
  group_by(component, file) %>%
  summarise(median_pct_missing = median(pct_missing), n_variables = n(), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(missing_by_file,
       aes(x = median_pct_missing, y = reorder(file, median_pct_missing), colour = component)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_variables)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Median % missing per variable (adults, n = 6,023)",
       y = "NHANES data file", colour = "Component", size = "Number of variables",
       title = "Missing values per NHANES data file")
```

## Why are they missing?

Most of the missing values are **missing by design** (planned missingness), not because of a measurement problem:

- **Subsamples**: some laboratory panels are measured only in a random subsample. The fasting panels (`TRIGLY_L`: triglycerides and LDL; `GLU_L`: fasting glucose; `INS_L`: insulin) are only measured in participants examined in the morning session after an overnight fast (~50% missing). Volatile organic compounds (`VOCWB_L`) and PFAS (`PFAS_L`) are measured in a random subsample of roughly 35–40% of the participants (~60–65% missing).
- **Age- or sex-specific components**: ferritin, transferrin receptor and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (`FERTIN_L`, `TFR_L`, `AGP_L`) and the urine pregnancy test are only measured in specific age/sex groups. The infant-feeding (`DBQ_L`) and early-childhood (`ECQ_L`) questions are about children and are therefore almost completely empty for adults.
- **Skip patterns** in questionnaires: for example, `ALQ130` (drinks per day) is only asked to people who drank alcohol in the past year.
- **Non-participation in a component**: 293 adults (4.9%) have no blood measurements (e.g. no blood draw). They are similar to the other participants in mean age (51.2 vs 54.2 years) and sex (54.3% vs 54.9% women).

Because subsample selection is random, the missingness in the subsample panels can be considered missing completely at random (MCAR) with respect to the participants' characteristics. Imputing a panel that is missing for 50–80% of the participants would mostly create artificial data. We therefore **do not impute**, but select variables with a low proportion of missing values (section 8) and use complete cases per analysis. The age and sex comparison for the missing blood draw:

```{r missing-blood}
nhanes %>%
  mutate(blood_measured = if_else(is.na(LBXGH), "No blood measurements", "Blood measured")) %>%
  group_by(blood_measured) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_age = mean(RIDAGEYR),
            pct_female = mean(sex == "Female") * 100)
```

# Selection of laboratory features

The 387 laboratory variables are the high-dimensional part of the dataset, and we will use them for the multiple testing study (part 3) and as candidate predictors (part 4). We select the informative ones in five steps. **None of these steps uses an outcome or group label** (such as obesity), which is required for part 3: the filter must not favour features that differ between the groups we will compare.

```{r lab-candidates}
lab_vars <- codebook %>%
  filter(component == "Laboratory") %>%
  mutate(
    # label without the unit between brackets, e.g. "Blood lead (ug/dL)" -> "Blood lead"
    base_label = str_trim(str_remove(label, "\\s*\\(.*\\)\\s*$")),
    is_weight  = str_starts(variable, "WT"),
    is_comment = str_detect(label, regex("comment|cmt|comt", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    is_fasting_question = file == "FASTQX_L"
  )
```

**Step 1: keep only measurements.** We remove sample weights (`WT...`), comment codes (detection-limit flags, used in step 4) and the fasting questionnaire (`FASTQX_L`: hours since the last meal; not a biological measurement).

**Step 2: remove unit duplicates.** Many analytes are reported twice, in conventional and SI units (e.g. `LBXTC` in mg/dL and `LBDTCSI` in mmol/L). These are perfectly correlated, so we keep the first one of each pair (same file, same label apart from the unit).

```{r lab-step1-2}
step1 <- lab_vars %>% filter(!is_weight, !is_comment, !is_fasting_question)
step2 <- step1 %>% filter(!duplicated(paste(file, base_label)))
```

**Step 3: less than 20% missing values.** This removes the subsample panels described in section 7, which would leave too few complete samples for multivariable analyses. The threshold falls in a natural gap: the remaining variables have at most 11% missing values, the next ones 33% (LDH) or more.

```{r lab-step3}
pct_missing_lab <- colMeans(is.na(nhanes[, step2$variable]))
step3 <- step2 %>% filter(pct_missing_lab[variable] < 0.20)
```

**Step 4: enough distinct values.** For each variable, we compute the proportion of participants with the most frequent value. When this proportion is above 30%, the variable is either categorical (e.g. hepatitis serology: positive/negative) or mostly below the limit of detection. NHANES replaces values below the detection limit by one fixed value, the detection limit divided by √2. Such variables carry little quantitative information.

```{r lab-step4}
modal_frequency <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  max(table(x)) / length(x)
}
modal_freq <- sapply(nhanes[, step3$variable], modal_frequency)

# Which variables are removed and why?
tibble(variable = names(modal_freq), modal_freq = round(modal_freq, 2)) %>%
  filter(modal_freq > 0.30) %>%
  left_join(codebook %>% select(variable, label), by = "variable") %>%
  arrange(modal_freq) %>%
  knitr::kable()

step4 <- step3 %>% filter(modal_freq[variable] <= 0.30)
```

**Step 5: detection limit and duplicate analytes.** For RBC folate forms, the detection limit depends on the sample, so values below it are not all identical and step 4 does not catch them. We therefore also look at the comment codes, which flag each value below the detection limit (code 1):

```{r lab-lod}
lod_tbl <- lab_vars %>%
  filter(is_comment) %>%
  mutate(pct_below_lod = map_dbl(variable, ~ mean(nhanes[[.x]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE) * 100)) %>%
  select(variable, label, pct_below_lod) %>%
  arrange(desc(pct_below_lod))

# Comment codes of the features that are still in the selection after step 4
lod_tbl %>%
  filter(variable %in% c("LBDRF2LC", "LBDRF3LC", "LBDRF5LC", "LBDTHGLC")) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

Folic acid and 5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate in red blood cells (`LBXRF2SI`, `LBXRF3SI`) are below the detection limit in more than half of the participants, so we remove them. For the other remaining features, at most 24% of the values are below the detection limit; we keep them.

Finally, total cholesterol was measured twice, in two different laboratory panels (`LBXTC` in `TCHOL_L` and `LBXSCH` in the biochemistry profile). These two measurements are almost identical, so we keep only `LBXTC`:

```{r lab-step5}
cor(nhanes$LBXTC, nhanes$LBXSCH, use = "complete.obs")

lab_features <- setdiff(step4$variable, c("LBXRF2SI", "LBXRF3SI", "LBXSCH"))
```

```{r lab-filter-summary}
tibble(
  step = c("All laboratory variables",
           "1. Measurements only (no weights, comment codes, fasting questions)",
           "2. No unit duplicates",
           "3. < 20% missing values",
           "4. Most frequent value in <= 30% of participants",
           "5. Not mostly below detection limit, no duplicate analyte"),
  n_variables = c(nrow(lab_vars), nrow(step1), nrow(step2), nrow(step3), nrow(step4),
                  length(lab_features))
) %>% knitr::kable()
```

We keep **101 laboratory features**. They cover complete blood count, biochemistry (liver and kidney function, electrolytes, lipids), glycohemoglobin, fatty acids, folate forms, vitamin D, sex hormones, metals, inflammation (CRP) and urine albumin/creatinine.

# Distributions and transformation

## Skewness

Most laboratory values are concentrations, which are typically right-skewed: many low values and a long tail of high values. Skewed variables violate the normality assumption of t-tests and linear models, and a few extreme values dominate the mean, the variance and the PCA. We quantify the asymmetry with the skewness: 0 for a symmetric distribution; above 1 indicates a strong right tail.

```{r skewness}
skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  m <- mean(x)
  s <- sqrt(mean((x - m)^2))
  mean((x - m)^3) / s^3
}

skew_before <- sapply(nhanes[, lab_features], skewness)
summary(skew_before)
sum(skew_before > 1)
```

## Log2 transformation

We log2-transform every feature with a skewness above 1 (`r sum(skew_before > 1)` of the `r length(lab_features)` features). On a log2 scale, a difference of 1 corresponds to a doubling of the concentration, which is easy to interpret (cf. log fold changes in the RNA-seq practical). One feature (eosinophil percentage) contains zeros; for that one, we add half of the smallest positive value before taking the log, similar to the pseudocount used for RNA-seq counts.

Features with a negative skewness (a tail to the left) are not log-transformed, because a log transformation would make the left tail longer.

```{r log-transform}
log_offset <- function(x) {
  if (min(x, na.rm = TRUE) > 0) 0 else min(x[x > 0], na.rm = TRUE) / 2
}

to_log <- names(skew_before)[skew_before > 1]

lab_log <- nhanes[, lab_features]
for (v in to_log) {
  lab_log[[v]] <- log2(lab_log[[v]] + log_offset(lab_log[[v]]))
}

skew_after <- sapply(lab_log, skewness)
sum(abs(skew_before) > 1)   # strongly skewed before
sum(abs(skew_after) > 1)    # strongly skewed after
```

```{r skew-plot}
tibble(variable = lab_features, before = skew_before, after = skew_after,
       transformed = lab_features %in% to_log) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = before, y = after, colour = transformed)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey50", "TRUE" = "#B2182B"),
                      labels = c("not transformed", "log2-transformed")) +
  labs(x = "Skewness before transformation", y = "Skewness after transformation",
       colour = NULL, title = "Skewness of the 101 laboratory features")
```

The log transformation removes most of the asymmetry: the number of strongly skewed features (|skewness| > 1) drops from 65 to 15. The remaining skewed features are mostly variables whose tail is caused by a clinical subgroup, not by the measurement scale. For glycohemoglobin (HbA1c) and serum glucose, the tail consists of people with diabetes. We keep this tail because it is biology, not error, and take it into account when we choose statistical tests later.

Example of three typical features before and after transformation:

```{r transform-examples, fig.height = 6}
examples <- c(LBXHSCRP = "C-reactive protein (mg/L)",
              LBXSGTSI = "Gamma-glutamyl transferase (IU/L)",
              LBXSTR   = "Triglycerides (mg/dL)")

bind_rows(
  nhanes[, names(examples)] %>% mutate(scale = "Original scale"),
  lab_log[, names(examples)] %>% mutate(scale = "log2 scale")
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-scale, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(variable = examples[variable],
         scale = factor(scale, levels = c("Original scale", "log2 scale"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(scale ~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of participants")
```

```{r qq-example, fig.height = 3.5}
ggarrange(
  ggqqplot(nhanes$LBXHSCRP[!is.na(nhanes$LBXHSCRP)], title = "CRP, original scale"),
  ggqqplot(lab_log$LBXHSCRP[!is.na(lab_log$LBXHSCRP)], title = "CRP, log2 scale"),
  ncol = 2
)
```

# Outliers

## Clinical measurements

Unlike the blood pressure values in the cardiovascular practical (with values such as 14/7 instead of 140/70), the clinical measurements here have no impossible values. The extremes are rare but physiologically possible:

```{r clinical-ranges}
nhanes %>%
  select(BMXBMI, BMXWT, BMXHT, BMXWAIST, sbp, dbp) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(value)), min = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
            median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE), max = max(value, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r clinical-boxplots, fig.height = 4}
nhanes %>%
  select(`BMI (kg/m²)` = BMXBMI, `Waist (cm)` = BMXWAIST,
         `Systolic BP (mmHg)` = sbp, `Diastolic BP (mmHg)` = dbp) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

As an internal consistency check, we recompute the BMI from the measured weight and height. The differences are smaller than 0.05 kg/m², i.e. only rounding:

```{r bmi-check}
bmi_recomputed <- nhanes$BMXWT / (nhanes$BMXHT / 100)^2
summary(abs(bmi_recomputed - nhanes$BMXBMI))
```

**Decision**: we keep all clinical values. A BMI of 74.8 or a systolic blood pressure of 232 mmHg is extreme but occurs in severe obesity and hypertension; removing these values would remove exactly the people that are clinically most relevant.

## Laboratory features

After log transformation, we count per feature how many values lie more than 5 standard deviations from the mean:

```{r lab-outliers}
lab_z <- scale(lab_log)
n_extreme <- colSums(abs(lab_z) > 5, na.rm = TRUE)
head(sort(n_extreme, decreasing = TRUE), 8)
```

The features with the most extreme values are biologically interpretable. HbA1c (`LBXGH`) and serum glucose (`LBXSGL`) are extreme in uncontrolled diabetes. Serum folic acid (`LBXSF2SI`) is extreme in people taking folic acid supplements, and estrone (`LBXESO`) in women using hormone therapy. These are true values, not technical errors, so **we keep them**. In the next parts we will check the influence of extreme observations, e.g. with Cook's distance (as in the statistics practical) or with rank-based or robust methods.

Whether whole *samples* behave unlike the rest is checked with the PCA in the next section.

# PCA: do samples cluster by biology or by technical factors?

We perform a PCA on the 101 log-transformed laboratory features. PCA requires complete data, so we use the 4,261 participants without any missing laboratory value (70.7% of the study population). The features have very different units, so they are standardised (mean 0, SD 1) with `scale. = TRUE`. Otherwise features with a large variance (e.g. platelet count) would dominate the components.

```{r pca}
pca_input <- lab_log %>%
  mutate(SEQN = nhanes$SEQN) %>%
  drop_na()

pca_res <- prcomp(pca_input %>% select(-SEQN), center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

pca_scores <- as_tibble(pca_res$x[, 1:10]) %>%
  mutate(SEQN = pca_input$SEQN) %>%
  left_join(nhanes %>% select(SEQN, RIDAGEYR, age_group, sex, race_eth, BMXBMI,
                              bmi_cat, exam_period, exam_session),
            by = "SEQN")

nrow(pca_scores)
```

## Explained variance

```{r scree}
tibble(pc = 1:20,
       pct_var = (pca_res$sdev^2 / sum(pca_res$sdev^2) * 100)[1:20]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pc, y = pct_var)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:20, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Principal component", y = "% of total variance explained",
       title = "Explained variance of the first 20 principal components")
```

The first components explain only a modest part of the variance (PC1 8.5%, PC2 6.5%, PC3 6.0%; 30% for the first five). This is expected: the panel combines many largely independent physiological systems (blood count, liver, kidney, hormones, nutrition), unlike e.g. a transcriptome where many genes are co-regulated.

## PC1 versus PC2, coloured by biological and technical factors

```{r pca-plots, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 11}
pca_plot <- function(colour_var, title) {
  ggplot(pca_scores %>% drop_na(all_of(colour_var)),
         aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = .data[[colour_var]])) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    labs(title = title, colour = NULL) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1)))
}

ggarrange(
  pca_plot("age_group", "Age group"),
  pca_plot("sex", "Sex"),
  pca_plot("bmi_cat", "BMI category"),
  pca_plot("exam_period", "Exam period (technical)"),
  pca_plot("exam_session", "Exam session (technical)"),
  ncol = 2, nrow = 3
)
```

## Which factors are associated with the principal components?

To quantify the plots, we fit a linear model of each of the first five components on each factor and report the R² (the proportion of the variance of the component explained by the factor).

```{r pca-association}
pc_factors <- c(Age = "RIDAGEYR", Sex = "sex", `Race/ethnicity` = "race_eth",
                BMI = "BMXBMI", `Exam period` = "exam_period", `Exam session` = "exam_session")

pc_assoc <- expand_grid(pc = paste0("PC", 1:5), factor = pc_factors) %>%
  mutate(r2 = map2_dbl(pc, factor, ~ summary(lm(reformulate(.y, response = .x),
                                                data = pca_scores))$r.squared),
         factor_label = names(pc_factors)[match(factor, pc_factors)])

ggplot(pc_assoc, aes(x = pc, y = factor_label, fill = r2)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#B2182B", limits = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = expression(R^2),
       title = "Association between principal components and participant characteristics")
```

BMI, the biology we care about, is not visible in PC1 and PC2 but in PC3 (see the table above). The PC3 scores shift steadily from normal weight to obesity. The sign of a principal component is arbitrary, so whether PC3 goes up or down with BMI has no meaning:

```{r pc3-bmi, fig.height = 4}
pca_scores %>%
  drop_na(bmi_cat) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bmi_cat, y = PC3)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85", outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "BMI category", y = "PC3",
       title = "The third principal component reflects body weight")
```

## Which features drive PC1 and PC2?

```{r loadings, fig.height = 6}
as_tibble(pca_res$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "variable") %>%
  left_join(codebook %>% select(variable, label), by = "variable") %>%
  pivot_longer(c(PC1, PC2), names_to = "pc", values_to = "loading") %>%
  group_by(pc) %>%
  slice_max(abs(loading), n = 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(label_pc = paste(pc, label, sep = ": ")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = loading, y = reorder(label_pc, abs(loading)))) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~ pc, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) str_remove(x, "^PC[0-9]+: ")) +
  labs(x = "Loading", y = NULL, title = "Top 10 features of PC1 and PC2")
```

**Interpretation.**

- **PC1 is mainly age** (R² = 0.35). It is driven by folate forms and vitamin D, which are higher in older adults, among other things because supplement use increases with age.
- **PC2 is mainly sex** (R² = 0.41). It is driven by hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, testosterone and serum iron, which are all higher in men.
- **PC3 is associated with BMI** (R² = 0.25). This is a first indication that body weight is linked to a broad laboratory profile, which we will study in parts 2 and 3.
- **The technical factors do not structure the data.** The exam period (winter vs summer) and the exam session (morning vs afternoon) explain at most about 1% of the variance of any of the first five components.
- No sample lies further than 5 standard deviations from the centre on PC1 or PC2. We therefore see no sign of technically failed samples.

The samples thus cluster by biology (age, sex, BMI), not by a technical batch factor. Because age and sex dominate the laboratory profile, **they are important potential confounders** and must be included as covariates in the analyses of parts 2 and 3.

# Correlation structure of the laboratory features

A clustered correlation heatmap shows which features carry overlapping information. This matters for interpreting multiple tests (part 3: tests on correlated features are not independent) and feature importance (part 4).

```{r cor-heatmap, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 10}
cor_mat <- cor(lab_log, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
lab_panel <- codebook$file[match(colnames(cor_mat), codebook$variable)]

Heatmap(cor_mat,
        name = "Pearson r",
        col = circlize::colorRamp2(c(-1, 0, 1), c("#2166AC", "white", "#B2182B")),
        top_annotation = HeatmapAnnotation(panel = lab_panel),
        show_column_names = FALSE,
        row_names_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 5),
        show_column_dend = FALSE,
        column_title = "Correlation between the 101 laboratory features (log2 scale where applied)")
```

The features form clear modules that correspond to physiological systems and laboratory panels: red blood cell indices, white blood cell counts, folate forms, fatty acids, sex hormones, and liver enzymes. Within these modules, correlations are high. The highest values (r ≈ 0.96–0.97, e.g. hemoglobin–hematocrit and the two RBC folate assays) are between closely related but distinct measurements, not between pure duplicates.

# Save the preprocessed data

We save two files for the next parts:

- `nhanes_clean.rds`: the study population (6,023 adults) with the recoded clinical variables and the 101 laboratory features on their **original** scale. The original scale is needed for clinical definitions, e.g. diabetes as HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.
- `nhanes_lab_log2.rds`: the same 101 laboratory features, **log2-transformed** where applicable, to be used for statistical testing and PCA.

A table with the selected features and their transformation is saved as `lab_features.csv`.

```{r save}
clinical_vars <- c("SEQN", "sex", "RIDAGEYR", "age_group", "race_eth", "education",
                   "INDFMPIR", "exam_period", "exam_session",
                   "BMXWT", "BMXHT", "BMXBMI", "bmi_cat", "obese", "BMXWAIST",
                   "abdominal_obese", "LBXCOT", "smoker",
                   "sbp", "dbp", "ALQ111", "ALQ121", "ALQ130")

nhanes_clean <- nhanes %>% select(all_of(clinical_vars), all_of(lab_features))
nhanes_lab_log2 <- lab_log %>% mutate(SEQN = nhanes$SEQN, .before = 1)

lab_info <- tibble(variable = lab_features) %>%
  left_join(codebook %>% select(variable, label, file), by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(pct_missing = round(colMeans(is.na(nhanes[, lab_features])) * 100, 1),
         skew_before = round(skew_before[variable], 2),
         log2_transformed = variable %in% to_log,
         skew_after = round(skew_after[variable], 2))

saveRDS(nhanes_clean, file.path(data_dir, "nhanes_clean.rds"))
saveRDS(nhanes_lab_log2, file.path(data_dir, "nhanes_lab_log2.rds"))
write_csv(lab_info, file.path(data_dir, "lab_features.csv"))

dim(nhanes_clean)
dim(nhanes_lab_log2)
```

# Summary: answers to the guiding questions

**How many samples and features, and which variable types?** The raw data contain 11,933 participants and 486 variables: 27 demographic, 32 examination, 387 laboratory and 40 questionnaire variables. 237 are numeric measurements (continuous, e.g. laboratory values and BMI, or discrete, e.g. age and number of drinks). 84 are binary or categorical codes: nominal, e.g. sex and race/ethnicity, or ordinal, e.g. education and alcohol frequency; these were converted to (ordered) factors. 155 are not features (identifier, survey design variables, comment codes), and 10 are constant or empty.

**Study population.** We analyse 6,023 non-pregnant adults (≥ 20 years) who were both interviewed and examined.

**Where are the missing values, why, and how did we handle them?** Most missingness is planned: subsample panels (fasting, PFAS, VOCs), age- or sex-specific components, and questionnaire skip patterns. It is therefore unrelated to the participants' characteristics. We did not impute. Instead, we selected laboratory features with less than 20% missing values and will use complete cases per analysis. Special codes (refused/don't know) were recoded to `NA`.

**Samples or features that behave unlike the rest?** Clinical extremes (BMI up to 74.8, systolic BP up to 232 mmHg) are plausible and kept. Extreme laboratory values correspond to clinical subgroups (diabetes, supplement or hormone use) and are kept. The PCA shows no outlying samples. Features that are mostly below the detection limit, categorical or duplicated were removed.

**Preprocessing steps.** Selection of 101 laboratory features with five label-independent filters; a log2 transformation of the 63 right-skewed features; standardisation within the PCA. Normalisation as for RNA-seq is not needed: each laboratory value is an absolute, calibrated concentration.

**Do samples cluster by biology or by a technical factor?** By biology. PC1 reflects age, PC2 sex and PC3 BMI, the biology of interest for our research question. The exam period and session explain at most about 1% of the variance of any of the first five components.

**Is the dataset suitable for the next parts?** Yes. For our research question (obesity), all variables are available: the outcome (BMI), the explanatory variables and confounders of part 2 (race/ethnicity, sex, age, income), the confounders of part 3 (age, sex, race/ethnicity, smoking) and the 101 laboratory features. There are 5,929 adults with a BMI (41.1% obese), 5,824 with a blood pressure measurement and 5,371–5,870 with each laboratory feature (4,261 with all 101 features). This is ample for multivariable models (part 2), a multiple testing study over 101 features (part 3) and a machine learning model with a separate test set (part 4). Age and sex must be included as covariates because they dominate the laboratory profile.

**Limitation.** NHANES uses a complex, stratified sampling design with oversampling of some groups. Flegal et al. used the sample weights (`WTMEC2YR`) to obtain estimates that represent the US population. We do not use these weights, so our results describe associations within this sample and are not population prevalence estimates.
